title: The nautilus shell is a perfect logarithmic spiral, but it is not a golden spiral

cover.alt: A nautilus shell cut in half, showing its chambers curling outwards in a smooth spiral.

body: Posters and textbooks love to lay a **golden spiral** over a nautilus shell, but the match is a myth. The shell really is one of nature's finest *logarithmic* spirals: each turn is a scaled-up copy of the last, so the animal keeps the same shape as it grows. A golden spiral is just one special logarithmic spiral, widening by the golden ratio (about 1.618) every quarter turn, and most mollusc shells, nautilus included, grow at noticeably different rates. The animal adds a new chamber as it grows and lives in the newest one, using the sealed older chambers for buoyancy.

slides.explanation: Logarithmic spirals keep their shape as they grow, as the nautilus does. The golden-spiral claim for shells and galaxies is often repeated but wrong.

slides.heading: What a golden spiral is
slides.text: A logarithmic spiral grows by the same factor for every equal turn. A [golden spiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_spiral) is the one that grows by the golden ratio, about 1.618, every quarter turn. Shells and galaxies grow logarithmically too, but usually at angles well away from that special case.

slides.alt: A living nautilus with a striped brown and white shell and many small tentacles, swimming in dark water.
slides.caption: A living nautilus from Palau. The animal occupies only the outermost chamber; the rest are sealed and gas-filled.

slides.heading: Nautilus numbers: higher or lower?
slides.note: Rounded figures from the Wikipedia article on nautiluses
slides.explanation: Adults have 30 or more chambers and up to 90-plus tentacles, mature at about 15 years, and nautiloids go back about 500 million years.
